**TRAPPIST-1** (also known as **2MASS J23062928−0502285** or **SPECULOOS-1**) is a [red dwarf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_dwarf "Red dwarf") star[\[b\]](#cite_note-19) with seven known [exoplanets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exoplanet "Exoplanet"). It lies in the constellation [Aquarius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquarius_\(constellation\) "Aquarius (constellation)") approximately 40.66 [light-years](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light-year "Light-year") (12.47 [pc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parsec "Parsec")) away from [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth"). An [ultra-cool dwarf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultra-cool_dwarf "Ultra-cool dwarf"), it has a surface temperature of about 2,566 [K](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelvin "Kelvin") (2,290 [°C](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celsius "Celsius"); 4,160 [°F](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fahrenheit "Fahrenheit")). Its radius is slightly larger than [Jupiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jupiter "Jupiter")'s and it has a mass of about 9% of [the Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_mass "Solar mass"). It is estimated to be 7.6 billion years old, making it older than the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System"). The discovery of the star was first published in 2000.

Observations in 2016 from [TRAPPIST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TRAPPIST "TRAPPIST")–South (Transiting Planets and Planetesimals Small Telescope project) at [La Silla Observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Silla_Observatory "La Silla Observatory") in Chile and other telescopes led to the discovery of two [terrestrial planets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrestrial_planet "Terrestrial planet") in orbit around TRAPPIST-1. In 2017, further analysis of the original observations identified five more terrestrial planets. The seven planets take between 1.5 and 19 days to [orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_period "Orbital period") the star in circular orbits. They are all likely [tidally locked](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tidally_locked "Tidally locked") to TRAPPIST-1, and it is therefore believed that each planet is in permanent day on one side and permanent night on the other. Their masses are comparable to that of Earth and they all lie in the same plane; seen from Earth, they pass in front of the star. This placement allowed the planets to be detected: when they pass in front of the star, its [apparent magnitude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apparent_magnitude "Apparent magnitude") dims.

Up to four of the planets—designated [*d*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TRAPPIST-1d "TRAPPIST-1d"), [*e*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TRAPPIST-1e "TRAPPIST-1e"), [*f*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TRAPPIST-1f "TRAPPIST-1f"), and [*g*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TRAPPIST-1g "TRAPPIST-1g")—orbit at distances where temperatures are likely suitable for the existence of liquid water, and are thus potentially hospitable to life. There is no evidence of an atmosphere on any of the planets, and observations of [TRAPPIST-1b](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TRAPPIST-1b "TRAPPIST-1b") have in particular ruled out the existence of an atmosphere. It is unclear whether radiation emissions from TRAPPIST-1 would allow for such atmospheres. The planets have low densities; they may consist of large amounts of [volatile material](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volatile_\(astrogeology\) "Volatile (astrogeology)"). Due to the possibility of several of the planets being habitable, the system has drawn interest from researchers and has appeared in popular culture.

## Discovery

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=TRAPPIST-1&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Discovery")\]

The star known as TRAPPIST-1 was discovered in 1999 by astronomer John Gizis and colleagues[\[18\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGizisMonetReidKirkpatrick20001088-20) during a [survey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two_Micron_All-Sky_Survey "Two Micron All-Sky Survey") of close-by [ultra-cool dwarf stars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultra-cool_dwarf "Ultra-cool dwarf").[\[19\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGillonJehinLedererDelrez2016225-21)[\[20\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGizisMonetReidKirkpatrick20001085-22) It appeared in sample C[\[18\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGizisMonetReidKirkpatrick20001088-20)[\[19\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGillonJehinLedererDelrez2016225-21) of the surveyed stars, which was obtained in June 1999. Publication of the discovery took place in 2000.[\[21\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGizisMonetReidKirkpatrick20001086-23) TRAPPIST-1 is named after [TRAPPIST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TRAPPIST "TRAPPIST") (the Transiting Planets and Planetesimals Small Telescope project),[\[13\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETurbetBolmontBourrierDemory20202-13)[\[c\]](#cite_note-27) which discovered the first two [exoplanets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exoplanet "Exoplanet") around the star.[\[25\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsmith2018118-28)

Its planetary system was discovered by a team led by [Michaël Gillon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michaël_Gillon "Michaël Gillon"), a Belgian astronomer[\[26\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERinaldiNúñez_Ferrer20171-29) at the [University of Liege](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Liege "University of Liege"),[\[27\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAngostoZaragozaMelón201785-30) in 2016[\[28\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAngostoZaragozaMelón201786-31) during observations made at the [La Silla Observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Silla_Observatory "La Silla Observatory"), Chile,[\[29\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarovShevchenko2020865-32)[\[30\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELinsky2019105-33) using the TRAPPIST telescope. The discovery was based on anomalies in the [light curves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_curve "Light curve")[\[d\]](#cite_note-35) measured by the telescope in 2015. These were initially interpreted as indicating the existence of three planets. In 2016, separate discoveries revealed that the third planet was in fact multiple planets. The telescopes and observatories involved were[\[13\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETurbetBolmontBourrierDemory20202-13) the [Spitzer Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spitzer_Space_Telescope "Spitzer Space Telescope") and the ground-based TRAPPIST–South, TRAPPIST–North in [Oukaïmeden Observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oukaïmeden_Observatory "Oukaïmeden Observatory"), Morocco, the [South African Astronomical Observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_Astronomical_Observatory "South African Astronomical Observatory"), and the [Liverpool Telescopes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool_Telescope "Liverpool Telescope") and [William Herschel Telescopes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Herschel_Telescope "William Herschel Telescope") in Spain.[\[32\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGillonTriaudDemoryJehin2017461-36)

The observations of TRAPPIST-1 are considered among the most important research findings of the [Spitzer Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spitzer_Space_Telescope "Spitzer Space Telescope").[\[33\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDucrot20214-37) Complementing the findings were observations by the [Himalayan Chandra Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Himalayan_Chandra_Telescope "Himalayan Chandra Telescope"), the [United Kingdom Infrared Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom_Infrared_Telescope "United Kingdom Infrared Telescope") and the [Very Large Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Very_Large_Telescope "Very Large Telescope").[\[34\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGillonJehinLedererDelrez2016221-38) Since then, research has confirmed the existence of at least seven planets in the system,[\[35\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETurbetBolmontBourrierDemory20203-39) the orbits of which have been calculated using measurements from the Spitzer and Kepler telescopes.[\[36\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAgolDornGrimmTurbet20212-40) Some news reports incorrectly attributed the discovery of the TRAPPIST-1 planets to [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA") alone; in fact the TRAPPIST project that led to their discovery received funding from both NASA and the [European Research Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Research_Council "European Research Council") of the [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union") (EU).[\[37\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERinaldiNúñez_Ferrer20171–2-41)

### Rotation period and age

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=TRAPPIST-1&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Rotation period and age")\]

Measurements of TRAPPIST-1's [rotation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stellar_rotation "Stellar rotation") have yielded a period of 3.3 days; earlier measurements of 1.4 days appear to have been caused by changes in the distribution of its [starspots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starspot "Starspot").[\[64\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoettenbacherKane20172-76) Its [rotational axis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotational_axis "Rotational axis") may be slightly offset from that of its planets.[\[65\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGüntherBerardoDucrotMurray202213-77)

Using a combination of techniques including composition and movements of the star, the age of TRAPPIST-1 has been estimated at about 7.6±2.2 billion years,[\[66\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurgasserMamajek20171-78) making it older than the Solar System, which is about 4.5 billion years old.[\[67\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEActonSlavneyArvidsonGaddis201732-79) It is expected to shine for ten trillion years—about 700 times[\[68\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESnellen2017423-80) longer than the present [age of the universe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_the_universe "Age of the universe")[\[69\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEActonSlavneyArvidsonGaddis201734-81)—whereas the Sun will run out of [hydrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen "Hydrogen") and leave the [main sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_sequence "Main sequence")[\[m\]](#cite_note-83) in a few billion years.[\[68\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESnellen2017423-80)

### Activity

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=TRAPPIST-1&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Activity")\]

Photospheric features have been detected on TRAPPIST-1[\[71\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorrisAgolHebbHawley20181-84) and probably make up a substantial part of the stellar surface.[\[72\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERathckeBuchhaveWitRackham20258-85) [James Webb Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Webb_Space_Telescope "James Webb Space Telescope") (JWST) observations indicate that cold starspots might cover up to one quarter of its photosphere.[\[73\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERadicaPiaulet-GhorayebTaylorCoulombe202511-86) The [Kepler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kepler_Space_Telescope "Kepler Space Telescope") and [Spitzer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spitzer_Space_Telescope "Spitzer Space Telescope") Space Telescopes have observed possible bright spots, which may be [faculae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_facula "Solar facula"),[\[n\]](#cite_note-88)[\[75\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorrisAgolDavenportHawley20185-89)[\[76\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELinsky2019250-90) although some of these may be too large to qualify as such.[\[77\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorrisAgolDavenportHawley20186-91) Bright spots are correlated to the occurrence of some [stellar flares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stellar_flare "Stellar flare").[\[o\]](#cite_note-93)[\[79\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGillonMeadowsAgolBurgasser20205-94) and their energy distribution resembles that of solar flares.[\[80\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVasilyevKostogryzShapiroVeronig20252-95) Kepler K2 observations have shown that TRAPPIST-1 produces frequent flares (42 flares in 80 days), including large, complex flares[\[81\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVidaKőváriPálOláh20172-96) that could alter nearby planetary atmospheres irreversibly and significantly, raising doubts of hosting life as we know it on Earth.[\[82\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVidaKőváriPálOláh20175-97)

The star has a strong [magnetic field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetic_field "Magnetic field")[\[83\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAirapetianBarnesCohenCollinson2020159-98) with a mean intensity of about 600 [gauss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss_\(unit\) "Gauss (unit)")[\[p\]](#cite_note-100)[\[85\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKochukhov202128-101) which may be an underestimate.[\[86\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavoudiRackhamGillonWit20242-102) The magnetic field drives high [chromospheric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromosphere "Chromosphere")[\[q\]](#cite_note-103)[\[83\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAirapetianBarnesCohenCollinson2020159-98) activity, and may be capable of trapping [coronal mass ejections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronal_mass_ejection "Coronal mass ejection").[\[r\]](#cite_note-105)[\[74\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGargaudAmilsQuintanillaCleaves2011Sun_\(and_Young_Sun\)-87)[\[87\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMullanPaudel20192-104)

According to Garraffo *et al.* (2017), TRAPPIST-1 loses about 3×10−14 solar masses per year[\[88\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESakaueShibata20211-106) to the [stellar wind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stellar_wind "Stellar wind"), a rate which is about 1.5 times that of the Sun.[\[89\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELinsky2019147–150-107) Dong *et al.* (2018) simulated the observed properties of TRAPPIST-1 with a mass loss of 4.1×10−15 solar masses per year.[\[88\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESakaueShibata20211-106) Simulations to estimate mass loss are complicated because, as of 2019, most of the parameters that govern TRAPPIST-1's stellar wind are not known from direct observation.[\[90\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFischerSaur20196-108)

## Planetary system

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=TRAPPIST-1&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Planetary system")\]

[![The TRAPPIST-1 system is about as compact as Jupiter's moons and much more than the Solar System](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/Comparison_of_the_TRAPPIST-1_system_with_the_inner_Solar_System_and_the_Galilean_Moons_of_Jupiter.jpg/330px-Comparison_of_the_TRAPPIST-1_system_with_the_inner_Solar_System_and_the_Galilean_Moons_of_Jupiter.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Comparison_of_the_TRAPPIST-1_system_with_the_inner_Solar_System_and_the_Galilean_Moons_of_Jupiter.jpg)

Comparison of the orbits of the TRAPPIST-1 planets with the Solar System and Jupiter's moons

TRAPPIST-1 is orbited by seven planets, designated [TRAPPIST-1b](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TRAPPIST-1b "TRAPPIST-1b"), [1c](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TRAPPIST-1c "TRAPPIST-1c"), [1d](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TRAPPIST-1d "TRAPPIST-1d"), [1e](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TRAPPIST-1e "TRAPPIST-1e"), [1f](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TRAPPIST-1f "TRAPPIST-1f"), [1g](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TRAPPIST-1g "TRAPPIST-1g") and [1h](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TRAPPIST-1h "TRAPPIST-1h")[\[91\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGonzalesFahertyGagnéTeske20192-109) in alphabetic order going out from the star.[\[s\]](#cite_note-112)[\[94\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVerasBreedt20172677-113) These planets have orbital periods ranging from 1.5 to 19 days,[\[9\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDelrezGillonTriaudDemory20183577–3597-9)[\[95\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAgolDornGrimmTurbet2021Tables-114)[\[96\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGrimmDemoryGillonDorn2018-115) at distances of 0.011–0.059 astronomical units[\[t\]](#cite_note-117) (1.7–8.9 million km).[\[98\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsmith2018120-118)

All the planets are much closer to their star than [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_\(planet\) "Mercury (planet)") is to the Sun,[\[28\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAngostoZaragozaMelón201786-31) with the distance between TRAPPIST-1b and 1c at [syzygy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syzygy_\(astronomy\) "Syzygy (astronomy)") being only twice that between the Earth and Moon,[\[99\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECooper2025112-119) making the TRAPPIST-1 system very compact.[\[100\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETurbetBolmontBourrierDemory20208-120) Kral *et al.* (2018) did not detect any [comets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comet "Comet") around TRAPPIST-1,[\[101\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKralWyattTriaudMarino20182650-121) and Marino *et al.* (2020) found no evidence of a [Kuiper belt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuiper_belt "Kuiper belt"),[\[102\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChildsMartinLivio20224-122) although it is uncertain whether a Solar System-like belt around TRAPPIST-1 would be observable from Earth.[\[103\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartinLivio20226-123) Observations with the [Atacama Large Millimeter Array](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Large_Millimeter_Array "Atacama Large Millimeter Array") found no evidence of a [circumstellar dust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circumstellar_dust "Circumstellar dust") disk.[\[104\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMarinoWyattKennedyKama20206071-124)

The inclinations of planetary orbits relative to each other are less than 0.1 degrees,[\[u\]](#cite_note-126)[\[106\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAgolDornGrimmTurbet202114-127) making TRAPPIST-1 the flattest planetary system in the [NASA Exoplanet Archive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_Exoplanet_Archive "NASA Exoplanet Archive").[\[107\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHeisingSasselovHernquistLuisa_Tió_Humphrey20211-128) The orbits are highly circular, with minimal [eccentricities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_eccentricity "Orbital eccentricity")[\[v\]](#cite_note-130)[\[100\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETurbetBolmontBourrierDemory20208-120) and are well aligned with the spin axis of TRAPPIST-1.[\[109\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDemoryPozuelosChewSabin202019-131) The planets orbit in the same plane and, from the perspective of the Solar System, transit TRAPPIST-1 during their orbit[\[110\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMaltagliati20171-132) and frequently pass in front of each other.[\[111\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaneJansenFauchezSelsis20211-133)

### Size and composition

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=TRAPPIST-1&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Size and composition")\]

The radii of the planets are estimated to range between 77.5+1.4  
−1.4% and 112.9+1.5  
−1.3% of Earth's radius.[\[112\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESrinivas201717-134) The planet/star mass ratio of the TRAPPIST-1 system resembles that of the moon/planet ratio of the Solar System's [gas giants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gas_giant "Gas giant").[\[113\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMadhusudhan2020p. 6-5-135)

The TRAPPIST-1 planets are expected to have compositions that resemble each other[\[114\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonoughYoshizaki20219-136) as well as that of Earth.[\[115\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELinsky2019198-137) The estimated densities of the planets are lower than Earth's[\[36\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAgolDornGrimmTurbet20212-40) which may imply that they have large amounts of [volatile chemicals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volatility_\(chemistry\) "Volatility (chemistry)").[\[w\]](#cite_note-139) Alternatively, their cores may be smaller than that of Earth and therefore they may be rocky planets with less iron than that of Earth,[\[117\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAgolDornGrimmTurbet202130-140)[\[118\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGillonMeadowsAgolBurgasser202011-141) include large amounts of elements other than iron,[\[119\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchlichtingYoung202216-142) or their iron may exist in an oxidised form rather than as a core.[\[118\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGillonMeadowsAgolBurgasser202011-141) Their densities are too low for a pure [magnesium silicate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnesium_silicate "Magnesium silicate") composition,[\[x\]](#cite_note-144) requiring the presence of lower-density compounds such as water.[\[121\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHakimRivoldiniVan_HoolstCottenier201870-145)[\[122\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarthCaroneBarnesNoack20211326-146) Planets b, d, f, g and h are expected to contain large quantities of volatile chemicals.[\[123\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGrimmDemoryGillonDorn20188-147) The planets may have deep atmospheres and oceans, and contain vast amounts of ice.[\[124\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELingamLoeb2021594-148) [Subsurface oceans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subsurface_ocean "Subsurface ocean"), buried under icy shells, would form in the colder planets.[\[125\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEQuickRobergeMendozaQuintana2023-149) Several compositions are possible considering the large uncertainties in their densities.[\[126\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVan_HoolstNoackRivoldini2019598-150) The photospheric features of the star may introduce inaccuracies in measurements of the properties of TRAPPIST-1's planets,[\[71\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorrisAgolHebbHawley20181-84) including their densities being underestimated by 8+20  
   \-7 per cent,[\[127\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELinsky2019253-151) and incorrect estimates of their water content.[\[128\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELinsky2019254-152)

### Resonance and tides

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=TRAPPIST-1&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Resonance and tides")\]

Animation of TRAPPIST-1 exoplanets transiting their host star, with effects on the star's light curve

The planets are in [orbital resonances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_resonance "Orbital resonance").[\[129\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAschwandenScholkmannBéthuneSchmutz20186-153) The durations of their orbits have ratios of 8:5, 5:3, 3:2, 3:2, 4:3 and 3:2 between neighbouring planet pairs,[\[130\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGrimmDemoryGillonDorn20183-154) and each set of three is in a [Laplace resonance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laplace_resonance "Laplace resonance").[\[y\]](#cite_note-156)[\[100\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETurbetBolmontBourrierDemory20208-120) [Simulations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N-body_simulation "N-body simulation") have shown such resonances can remain stable over billions of years but that their stability is strongly dependent on initial conditions. Many configurations become unstable after less than a million years. The resonances enhance the exchange of [angular momentum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angular_momentum "Angular momentum") between the planets, resulting in measurable variations—earlier or later—in their transit times in front of TRAPPIST-1. These variations yield information on the planetary system,[\[132\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGrimmDemoryGillonDorn20182-157) such as the masses of the planets, when other techniques are not available.[\[133\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDucrot20215-158) The resonances and the proximity to the host star have led to comparisons between the TRAPPIST-1 system and the [Galilean moons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilean_moon "Galilean moon") of Jupiter.[\[110\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMaltagliati20171-132) [Kepler-223](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kepler-223 "Kepler-223") is another exoplanet system with a TRAPPIST-1-like long resonance.[\[134\]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeadowsSchmidt20204-159)

# James Webb Space Telescope

Webb is the premier observatory of the next decade, serving thousands of astronomers worldwide. It studies every phase in the history of our Universe.

Active Mission

[Featured Content](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/webb/#Featured-Image)

[Latest News](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/webb/#Latest-News)

[Latest Images](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/webb/#Latest-Images)

![](https://science.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/jwst_artist_concept_0.png?w=1041)

Webb studies every phase in the history of our Universe, ranging from the first luminous glows after the Big Bang, to the formation of solar systems capable of supporting life on planets like Earth, to the evolution of our own Solar System. Webb launched on Dec. 25th 2021. It does not orbit around the Earth like the Hubble Space Telescope, it orbits the Sun 1.5 million kilometers (1 million miles) away from the Earth at what is called the second Lagrange point or L2.

**TRAPPIST-1e** is a [tidally locked](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tidally_locked "Tidally locked"), [rocky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrestrial_planet "Terrestrial planet"), close-to-Earth-sized [exoplanet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exoplanet "Exoplanet") orbiting within the [habitable zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habitable_zone "Habitable zone") around the [ultra-cool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultra-cool_dwarf "Ultra-cool dwarf") [red dwarf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_dwarf "Red dwarf") star [TRAPPIST-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TRAPPIST-1 "TRAPPIST-1"), located 40.7 [light-years](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light-year "Light-year") (12.5 [parsecs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parsec "Parsec"); 385 [trillion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1000000000000_\(number\) "1000000000000 (number)") [kilometers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilometre "Kilometre"); 239 trillion [miles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mile "Mile")) away from Earth in the constellation of [Aquarius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquarius_\(constellation\) "Aquarius (constellation)"). Astronomers used the [transit method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transit_method "Transit method") to find the exoplanet, a method that measures the dimming of a star when a planet crosses in front of it.

The planet was one of seven planets discovered orbiting the star using observations from the [Spitzer Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spitzer_Space_Telescope "Spitzer Space Telescope").[\[1\]](#cite_note-Gillon2017-1)[\[7\]](#cite_note-Gillon-Jehin-etal-2016-7) Three of seven planets (*e*, *f*, and *g*) are in the habitable zone.[\[8\]](#cite_note-8)[\[9\]](#cite_note-9) TRAPPIST-1e is similar to Earth's mass, radius, density, gravity, temperature, and stellar flux.[\[3\]](#cite_note-Grimm-Demory-etal-2018-3)[\[10\]](#cite_note-Delrez-2018-10) It is also confirmed that TRAPPIST-1e lacks a cloud-free [hydrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen "Hydrogen")\-dominated [atmosphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmosphere "Atmosphere"), meaning that if the planet has an atmosphere it is more likely to have a compact atmosphere like the terrestrial planets in the Solar System.[\[11\]](#cite_note-deWit-Wakeford-etal-2018-11)

In November 2018, researchers determined that of the seven exoplanets in the multi-planetary system, TRAPPIST-1e has the best chance of being an Earth-like [ocean planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ocean_planet "Ocean planet"), and the one most worthy of further study regarding habitability.[\[12\]](#cite_note-12) The most recent observation in 2025 was unable to conclude with confidence if there was an atmosphere or not, though it could rule out certain atmosphere scenarios.

## Physical characteristics

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=TRAPPIST-1e&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Physical characteristics")\]

### Mass, radius, density, composition, and temperature

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=TRAPPIST-1e&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Mass, radius, density, composition, and temperature")\]

TRAPPIST-1e was detected with the [transit method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transit_method "Transit method"), where the planet blocked a small percentage of its host star's light when passing between it and Earth. This allowed scientists to accurately determine the planet's radius at 0.920 [*R*🜨](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth_radius "Earth radius"), with a small uncertainty of about 83 km (52 mi). Transit-timing variations and advanced computer simulations helped constrain the planet's mass, which turned out to be 0.692 [*M*🜨](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth_mass "Earth mass"), or about 15% less massive than [Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus "Venus").[\[2\]](#cite_note-Agol2021-2) TRAPPIST-1e has 82% the surface gravity of Earth, the third lowest in the system. Its radius and mass are also the third least among the TRAPPIST-1 planets.[\[2\]](#cite_note-Agol2021-2)

With both the radius and mass of TRAPPIST-1e determined with low error margins, scientists could accurately calculate the planet's [density](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Density "Density"), [surface gravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface_gravity "Surface gravity"), and composition. Initial density estimates in 2018 suggested it has a density of 5.65 g/cm3, about 1.024 times Earth's density of 5.51 g/cm3. TRAPPIST-1e appeared to be unusual in its system, as it was the only planet with a density consistent with a pure rock-[iron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron "Iron") composition, and the only one with a higher density than Earth ([TRAPPIST-1c](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TRAPPIST-1c "TRAPPIST-1c") also appeared to be entirely rock, but with a lower density than TRAPPIST-1e). The higher density of TRAPPIST-1e implies an Earth-like composition and a solid rocky surface. This also appeared to be unusual among the TRAPPIST-1 planets, as most were thought to have densities consistent with being completely covered in either a thick steam/hot [CO2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_dioxide "Carbon dioxide") atmosphere, a [global liquid ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ocean_planet "Ocean planet"), or an ice shell.[\[3\]](#cite_note-Grimm-Demory-etal-2018-3) However, refined estimates show that all planets in the system have similar densities, consistent with rocky compositions, with TRAPPIST-1e having a somewhat lower but still Earth-like bulk density.[\[2\]](#cite_note-Agol2021-2)

The planet has a calculated [equilibrium temperature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equilibrium_temperature "Equilibrium temperature") of 246.1 [K](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelvin "Kelvin") (−27.1 [°C](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celsius "Celsius"); −16.7 [°F](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fahrenheit "Fahrenheit")) given an albedo of 0, also known as its "blackbody" temperature.[\[10\]](#cite_note-Delrez-2018-10) For a more realistic Earth-like [albedo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albedo "Albedo"), however, this provides an unrealistic picture of the surface temperature of the planet. Earth's equilibrium temperature is 255 K;[\[13\]](#cite_note-13)\[*[better source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Questionable_sources "Wikipedia:Verifiability")*\] it is Earth's greenhouse gases that raise its surface temperatures to the levels we experience. If TRAPPIST-1e has a thick atmosphere, its surface could be much warmer than its equilibrium temperature.

### Host star

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=TRAPPIST-1e&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Host star")\]

Main article: [TRAPPIST-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TRAPPIST-1 "TRAPPIST-1")

The planet orbits an ultracool dwarf star named TRAPPIST-1. The star has a mass of 0.09 M☉ and a radius of 0.12 *R*☉, near the boundary between that of a [brown dwarf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_dwarf "Brown dwarf") and low-mass star. It has a temperature of 2,566 K (2,293 °C; 4,159 °F) and is 7.6 billion years old. In comparison, the [Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun "Sun") is 4.6 billion years old[\[14\]](#cite_note-14) and has a temperature of 5,778 K (5,505 °C; 9,941 °F).[\[15\]](#cite_note-15) The star is metal-rich, with a [metallicity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metallicity "Metallicity") (\[Fe/H\]) of 0.04, or 109% the solar amount. This is particularly odd as such low-mass stars near the boundary between brown dwarfs and hydrogen-fusing stars should be expected to have considerably less metal content than the Sun. Its luminosity ([L☉](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_luminosity "Solar luminosity")) is 0.0566% of that of the Sun.

The star's [apparent magnitude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apparent_magnitude "Apparent magnitude"), or how bright it appears from Earth's perspective, is 18.8. Therefore, it is far too dim to be seen with the naked eye.

### Orbit

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=TRAPPIST-1e&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Orbit")\]

TRAPPIST-1e orbits its host star quite closely. One full revolution around TRAPPIST-1 takes only 6.10 days (~146 hours) to complete. It orbits at a distance of 0.0293 [AU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronomical_unit "Astronomical unit") (4.38 million km; 2.72 million mi), or just under 3% the separation between Earth and the [Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun "Sun"). For comparison, the closest planet in the Solar System, [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_\(planet\) "Mercury (planet)"), takes 88 days to orbit the Sun at a distance of 0.38 AU (57 million km; 35 million mi). It is in 3:2 [resonance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_resonance "Orbital resonance") with [TRAPPIST-1f](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TRAPPIST-1f "TRAPPIST-1f") and 3:2 resonance with [TRAPPIST-1d](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TRAPPIST-1d "TRAPPIST-1d"). Despite its close proximity to its host star, TRAPPIST-1e gets only about 60% the starlight that Earth gets from the Sun due to the low luminosity of its star. The star would cover an angular diameter of about 2.17 degrees from the surface of the planet, and so would appear about four times larger than the Sun does from Earth.

### Atmosphere

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=TRAPPIST-1e&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Atmosphere")\]

Transit observations with [James Webb Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Webb_Space_Telescope "James Webb Space Telescope") suggested no clear answer about the existence of an atmosphere, but it did rule out many atmosphere scenarios. See the "Habitability" studies below.

## Habitability

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=TRAPPIST-1e&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Habitability")\]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ee/Artist%E2%80%99s_impression_of_view_from_one_of_the_middle_planets_in_the_TRAPPIST-1_system.jpg/330px-Artist%E2%80%99s_impression_of_view_from_one_of_the_middle_planets_in_the_TRAPPIST-1_system.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Artist’s_impression_of_view_from_one_of_the_middle_planets_in_the_TRAPPIST-1_system.jpg)

Artist's impression of the TRAPPIST-1 system, seen from above the surface of one of the planets in the habitable zone

See also: [Habitability of red dwarf systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habitability_of_red_dwarf_systems "Habitability of red dwarf systems")

The exoplanet was announced to be orbiting within the habitable zone of its parent star, the region where, with the correct conditions and atmospheric properties, liquid water may exist on the surface of the planet. TRAPPIST-1e has a radius of around 0.91 R🜨, so it is likely a rocky planet. Its host star is an ultracool red dwarf, with only about 8% of the mass of the Sun (close to the boundary between brown dwarfs and hydrogen-fusing stars). As a result, stars like TRAPPIST-1 have the potential to remain stable for up to 12 trillion years, which is over 2,000 times longer than the Sun.[\[16\]](#cite_note-16) Because of this ability to live for such a long period of time, it is likely TRAPPIST-1 will be one of the last remaining stars in the Universe, when the [gas needed to form new stars will be exhausted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Future_of_an_expanding_universe#Degenerate_Era "Future of an expanding universe"), and the existing stars begin to die off.

### 2018 studies

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=TRAPPIST-1e&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 2018 studies")\]

Despite being likely [tidally locked](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tidally_locked "Tidally locked") meaning one hemisphere permanently faces the star while the other does not which may reduce the habitability of the planet, more detailed studies of TRAPPIST-1e and the other TRAPPIST-1 planets released in 2018 determined that the planet is in fact one of the most Earth-sized worlds found, with 91% the radius, 77% the mass, 102.4% the density (5.65 g/cm3), and 93% the surface gravity. TRAPPIST-1e is confirmed to be a terrestrial planet with a solid, rocky surface. It is cool enough for liquid water to pool on the surface, but not so cold that it would freeze like on [TRAPPIST-1f](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TRAPPIST-1f "TRAPPIST-1f"), [g](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TRAPPIST-1g "TRAPPIST-1g"), and [h](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TRAPPIST-1h "TRAPPIST-1h").[\[3\]](#cite_note-Grimm-Demory-etal-2018-3)

The planet receives a stellar flux 60.4% that of Earth, about a third lower than that of Earth but significantly more than that of [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars "Mars").[\[10\]](#cite_note-Delrez-2018-10) Its equilibrium temperature ranges from 225 K (−48 °C; −55 °F)[\[17\]](#cite_note-17) to 246.1 K (−27.1 °C; −16.7 °F),[\[10\]](#cite_note-Delrez-2018-10) depending on how much light the planet reflects into space. Both of these are between those of Earth and Mars as well. In addition, its atmosphere is confirmed to not be dense or thick enough to harm the habitability potential as well, according to models by the [University of Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington "University of Washington").[\[11\]](#cite_note-deWit-Wakeford-etal-2018-11) The atmosphere, if it is dense enough, may also help to transfer additional heat to the dark side of the planet.

### 2024 studies

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=TRAPPIST-1e&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 2024 studies")\]

According to a 2024 study, based on modeling, TRAPPIST-1e could be having its atmosphere stripped by its host star, possibly as a result of its short orbital period, which would make it inhospitable to life. The same phenomenon could impact the atmospheres of the other planets in this system.[\[18\]](#cite_note-Cohen2024-18)[\[19\]](#cite_note-space.com-19)

### 2025 studies

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=TRAPPIST-1e&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: 2025 studies")\]

Based on four observations of TRAPPIST-1e using the [James Webb Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Webb_Space_Telescope "James Webb Space Telescope")'s [NIRSpec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NIRSpec "NIRSpec") instrument, researchers were unable to find conclusive evidence for or against the presence of an atmosphere. The analysis showed two models the data could adequately explain. The first is a flat-line model, which could mean two things: TRAPPIST-1e is a bare rock; or it has an atmosphere of an unknown type completely hidden by a high, thick [cloud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloud "Cloud") deck. The second model is a range of [nitrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen "Nitrogen")\-rich atmospheres, with nitrogen as the dominant gas. Within the nitrogen scenarios, there is a "tentative preference" for trace amounts of [methane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methane "Methane") (CH4) mixed in. The authors conclude that the primary limitation in studying TRAPPIST-1e is mitigating the effects of its active star. To overcome this, a new program of 15 additional JWST observations is underway. This program will observe back-to-back transits of TRAPPIST-1e and its neighboring planet, [TRAPPIST-1b](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TRAPPIST-1b "TRAPPIST-1b"), which is believed to be a bare rock. By using the signal from the bare rock planet to correct for the star's activity, it may be possible to reveal whether TRAPPIST-1e has an atmosphere.[\[6\]](#cite_note-Glidden2025-6)[\[20\]](#cite_note-20)

## Discovery

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=TRAPPIST-1e&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Discovery")\]

A team of astronomers headed by Michaël Gillon[\[21\]](#cite_note-21) used the [TRAPPIST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TRAPPIST "TRAPPIST") (Transiting Planets and Planetesimals Small Telescope) telescope at the [La Silla Observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Silla_Observatory "La Silla Observatory") in the [Atacama Desert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atacama_Desert "Atacama Desert"), [Chile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chile "Chile"),[\[22\]](#cite_note-Guardian-2016-05-02-22) to observe TRAPPIST-1 and search for orbiting planets. By utilising [transit photometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transit_photometry "Transit photometry"), they discovered three Earth-sized planets orbiting the dwarf star; the innermost two are tidally locked to their host star while the outermost appears to lie either within the system's [habitable zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circumstellar_habitable_zone "Circumstellar habitable zone") or just outside of it.[\[23\]](#cite_note-23)[\[24\]](#cite_note-24) The team made their observations from September–December 2015 and published its findings in the May 2016 issue of the journal *[Nature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nature_\(journal\) "Nature (journal)")*.[\[7\]](#cite_note-Gillon-Jehin-etal-2016-7)[\[22\]](#cite_note-Guardian-2016-05-02-22)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d8/PIA22093-TRAPPIST-1-PlanetLineup-20180205.jpg/500px-PIA22093-TRAPPIST-1-PlanetLineup-20180205.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:PIA22093-TRAPPIST-1-PlanetLineup-20180205.jpg)

Artist's impression of the TRAPPIST-1 planetary system

The original claim and presumed size of the planet was revised when the full seven-planet system was revealed in 2017:

"We already knew that TRAPPIST-1, a small, faint star some 40 light-years away, was special. In May 2016, a team led by Michaël Gillon at Belgium’s University of Liege announced it was closely orbited by three planets that are probably rocky: TRAPPIST-1b, c and d ...

"As the team kept watching shadow after shadow cross the star, three planets no longer seemed like enough to explain the pattern. "At some point we could not make sense of all these transits," Gillon said.

"Now, after using the space-based Spitzer telescope to stare at the system for almost three weeks straight, Gillon and his team have solved the problem: TRAPPIST-1 has four more planets.

"The planets closest to the star, TRAPPIST-1b and c, are unchanged. But there's a new third planet, which has taken the d moniker, and what had looked like d before turned out to be glimpses of e, f, and g. There's a planet h, too, drifting farthest out, and only spotted once."[\[25\]](#cite_note-25)

**TRAPPIST-1f** is an [exoplanet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exoplanet "Exoplanet"), likely [rocky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocky_planet "Rocky planet"),[\[2\]](#cite_note-Agol2021-2) orbiting within the [habitable zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habitable_zone "Habitable zone")[\[5\]](#cite_note-5) around the [ultra-cool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultra-cool_dwarf "Ultra-cool dwarf") [red dwarf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_dwarf "Red dwarf") star [TRAPPIST-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TRAPPIST-1 "TRAPPIST-1"), located 40.7 [light-years](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light-year "Light-year") (12.5 [parsecs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parsec "Parsec")) away from Earth in the constellation of [Aquarius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquarius_\(constellation\) "Aquarius (constellation)"). The planet is likely [tidally locked](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tidal_locking "Tidal locking"), and has been as an [eyeball planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eyeball_planet "Eyeball planet") candidate.

## Physical characteristics

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=TRAPPIST-1f&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Physical characteristics")\]

### Mass, radius, and temperature

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=TRAPPIST-1f&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Mass, radius, and temperature")\]

TRAPPIST-1f is an [Earth-sized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrestrial_planet "Terrestrial planet") exoplanet, meaning it has a radius and mass close to that of Earth. It has an [equilibrium temperature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_equilibrium_temperature "Planetary equilibrium temperature") of 218 K (−55 °C; −67 °F).[\[4\]](#cite_note-Ducrot2020-4) It has a radius of 1.045 [*R*🜨](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth_radius "Earth radius") and a mass of 1.039 [*M*🜨](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth_mass "Earth mass").[\[2\]](#cite_note-Agol2021-2) It was initially estimated to have a much lower mass, and thus a low density of 3.3±0.9 g/cm3 and a [surface gravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface_gravity "Surface gravity") around 6.1 m/s2 (62% of Earth's value).[\[1\]](#cite_note-Gillon2017-1) This suggested a large amount of [volatiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volatile_\(astrogeology\) "Volatile (astrogeology)"), with a 2017 study suggesting that a water ocean may comprise as much as 20% of the planet's mass, increasing the temperature at the bottom of such an ocean to above 1,400 K (1,130 °C; 2,060 °F).[\[6\]](#cite_note-Itisdeadjimdead2017-6) However, refined density estimates show that TRAPPIST-1f, like other planets in the system, is only slightly less dense than Earth, consistent with a rocky composition.[\[2\]](#cite_note-Agol2021-2)

### Atmosphere

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=TRAPPIST-1f&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Atmosphere")\]

According to simulations of magma ocean-atmosphere interaction, TRAPPIST-1f is likely to retain a fraction of primordial steam atmosphere during the initial stages of evolution, and therefore today is likely to possess a thick ocean covered by atmosphere rich in abiotic oxygen.[\[7\]](#cite_note-7) Helium emission from TRAPPIST-1f (and planets b and e) has not been detected as of 2022.[\[8\]](#cite_note-8)

### Host star

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=TRAPPIST-1f&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Host star")\]

Main article: [TRAPPIST-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TRAPPIST-1 "TRAPPIST-1")

The planet orbits an ultracool dwarf star named TRAPPIST-1. The star has a mass of 0.09 M☉ and a radius of 0.12 *R*☉. It has a temperature of 2,566 K (2,293 °C; 4,159 °F) and is at least 7.6 billion years old. In comparison, the [Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun "Sun") is 4.6 billion years old[\[9\]](#cite_note-9) and has a temperature of 5,778 K.[\[10\]](#cite_note-10) The star is metal-rich, with a [metallicity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metallicity "Metallicity") (\[Fe/H\]) of 0.04, or 109% the solar amount. This is particularly odd as such low-mass stars near the boundary between [brown dwarfs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_dwarf "Brown dwarf") and hydrogen-fusing stars should be expected to have considerably less metal content than the Sun; on the other hand, metal-rich stars are also more likely to have planets than metal-poor ones. Its luminosity ([L☉](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_luminosity "Solar luminosity")) is 0.05% of that of the Sun.

The star's [apparent magnitude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apparent_magnitude "Apparent magnitude"), or how bright it appears from Earth's perspective, is 18.8. Therefore, it is too dim to be seen with the naked eye.

### Orbit

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=TRAPPIST-1f&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Orbit")\]

TRAPPIST-1f orbits its host star with an orbital period of about 9.21 days and an orbital distance of about 0.0385 [AU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronomical_unit "Astronomical unit") (5.76 million [km](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilometre "Kilometre"); 3.58 million [mi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mile "Mile")) compared to the distance of [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_\(planet\) "Mercury (planet)") from the Sun, which is about 0.38 AU. It is in 4:3 [resonance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_resonance "Orbital resonance") with [TRAPPIST-1g](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TRAPPIST-1g "TRAPPIST-1g") and 3:2 resonance with [TRAPPIST-1e](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TRAPPIST-1e "TRAPPIST-1e").

## Habitability

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=TRAPPIST-1f&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Habitability")\]

See also: [Habitability of red dwarf systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habitability_of_red_dwarf_systems "Habitability of red dwarf systems")

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0e/PIA21423_-_Surface_of_TRAPPIST-1f.jpg/250px-PIA21423_-_Surface_of_TRAPPIST-1f.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:PIA21423_-_Surface_of_TRAPPIST-1f.jpg)

Artist's impression of the surface of TRAPPIST-1f, depicting a liquid water ocean on its surface. The parent star and neighbouring planets are also illustrated.

The exoplanet was announced to be either orbiting within or slightly outside of the habitable zone of its parent star, the region where, with the correct conditions and atmospheric properties, liquid water may exist on the surface of the planet. On 31 August 2017, astronomers at the [Hubble Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Space_Telescope "Hubble Space Telescope") reported the first evidence of possible water content on the TRAPPIST-1 exoplanets.[\[11\]](#cite_note-HST-20170831-11)[\[12\]](#cite_note-TIE-20170904-12)

TRAPPIST-1f has a radius about the same as Earth, at around 1.045 R🜨, but was initially thought to have only about two thirds of Earth's mass, at around 0.68 M🜨. So, it was considered somewhat unlikely to be a fully rocky planet, and extremely unlikely to be an Earth-like one, that is rocky with a large iron core but without a thick hydrogen-helium atmosphere enveloping the planet. Simulations in 2017 suggested the planet is approximately 20% water by composition, much higher than that of Earth. With such a massive water envelope, the pressure and temperature will be high enough to keep the water in a gaseous state and any liquid water will only exist as clouds near the top of TRAPPIST-1f's atmosphere. Based on this study, TRAPPIST-1f is therefore likely to be no more habitable than any other [ice giant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice_giant "Ice giant") with water clouds in its atmosphere.[\[6\]](#cite_note-Itisdeadjimdead2017-6) However, refined estimates show that TRAPPIST-1f has about the same mass as Earth, and like other planets in the system, is only slightly less dense than Earth, consistent with a rocky composition.[\[2\]](#cite_note-Agol2021-2)

Its host star is an ultracool red dwarf, with only about 8% of the mass of the Sun (close to the boundary between brown dwarfs and hydrogen-fusing stars). As a result, stars like TRAPPIST-1 have the ability to live up to 4–5 trillion years, 400–500 times longer than the Sun will live.[\[13\]](#cite_note-Adams2004-13) Because of this ability to live for long periods of time, it is likely TRAPPIST-1 will be one of the last remaining stars when the Universe is much older than it is now, when [the gas needed to form new stars will be exhausted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Future_of_an_expanding_universe#Degenerate_Era "Future of an expanding universe"), and the remaining ones begin to die off.

The planet is very likely tidally locked, with one hemisphere permanently facing towards the star, while the opposite side shrouded in eternal darkness. However, between these two intense areas, there would be a sliver of moderate temperature – called the [terminator line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terminator_line "Terminator line"), where the temperatures may be suitable (about 273 K or 0 °C or 32 °F) for liquid water to exist. Additionally, a much larger portion of the planet may be habitable if it supports a thick enough atmosphere to transfer heat to the side facing away from the star.

> Abstract:Dimensionality plays a crucial role in long-range dipole-dipole interactions (DDIs). We demonstrate that a resonant nanophotonic structure modifies the apparent dimensionality in an interacting ensemble of emitters, as revealed by population decay dynamics. Our measurements on a dense ensemble of interacting quantum emitters in a resonant nanophotonic structure with long-range DDIs reveal an effective dimensionality reduction to $\\bar{d} = 2.20 (12)$, despite the emitters being distributed in 3D. This contrasts the homogeneous environment, where the apparent dimension is $\\bar{d} = 3.00$. Our work presents a promising avenue to manipulate dimensionality in an ensemble of interacting emitters.

> Abstract:Structural transformation, the shift from agrarian economies to more diversified industrial and service-based systems, is a key driver of economic development. However, in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), data scarcity and unreliability hinder accurate assessments of this process. This paper presents a novel statistical framework designed to address these challenges by integrating Bayesian hierarchical modeling, machine learning-based data imputation, and factor analysis. The framework is specifically tailored for conditions of data sparsity and is capable of providing robust insights into sectoral productivity and employment shifts across diverse economies. By utilizing Bayesian models, uncertainties in data are effectively managed, while machine learning techniques impute missing data points, ensuring the integrity of the analysis. Factor analysis reduces the dimensionality of complex datasets, distilling them into core economic structures. The proposed framework has been validated through extensive simulations, demonstrating its ability to predict structural changes even when up to 60\\% of data is missing. This approach offers policymakers and researchers a valuable tool for making informed decisions in environments where data quality is limited, contributing to the broader understanding of economic development in LMICs.

## A Symposia Report on TRAPPIST-1e and K2-18b

---

**Prepared for the International Astrobiology Symposia**

**October 2026**

**Author:** [Your Name / Redacted]

**Institution:** [Redacted]

### Keywords: exoplanet habitability; James Webb Space Telescope; TRAPPIST-1e; K2-18b; atmospheric characterization; Hycean worlds; ultracool dwarf stars

---

### EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has fundamentally transformed the study of exoplanet atmospheres, enabling direct chemical probes of habitability-relevant worlds for the first time. This report presents a comparative analysis of two emblematic targets: **TRAPPIST-1e**, an Earth-sized rocky planet orbiting within the habitable zone (HZ) of an ultracool M8V dwarf star; and **K2-18b**, a sub-Neptune/hycean-type world residing in the HZ of a brighter M3V star. While JWST's NIRSpec observations of TRAPPIST-1e have yielded inconclusive but constraining results — ruling out hydrogen-dominated atmospheres while leaving open the possibility of bare rock, cloudy skies, or nitrogen-rich compositions — K2-18b has shown tantalizing spectroscopic evidence for carbon-bearing molecules including methane (CH₄) and carbon dioxide (CO₂), with a tentative ~3$\sigma$ signal attributed to dimethyl sulfide (DMS). This report synthesizes all published JWST findings through September 2025, contextualizes them within stellar-environment considerations, presents comparative physical parameter tables, and discusses the scientific pathway forward.
